transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-03-31 15:00 PDT
Duration: 42 minutes
Attendees: Dana Morris (Redwood AE), Sameer Patel (Redwood SE), Priya Rao (SageBridge CTO), Ellen Park (ML Lead), Marco Diaz (Infra)
---
Summary: quick POC check-in to review last week's throughput/cost numbers, discuss caching anomalies, and agree next experiments and owners. Decent progress on prefix caching, some unexpected token inflation on long-context threads.

[00:00] Dana: ok hi everyone, thanks for joining, we got a pretty packed agenda but mostly a short sync, I want to kick it off, quick updates and then Sameer will walk through the numbers.
[00:12] Priya: hey, thanks Dana, we only have Ellen and Marco on the call from our side, hey team.
[00:18] Sameer: cool yeah I'll share screen in a sec, um, but quick TL;DR: tokens/sec per dollar improved by about 22% after the caching tweaks, but tail latency bumped on a 32k long-context path, so tradeoffs to discuss.
[00:35] Ellen: right, we saw, I mean, caching definitely helped on FAQ-like flows, our hit-rate for the 5k prefix test jumped to ~68% from 44, which was great, but the multi-turn long threads where they keep appending logs, the kv cache invalidates more often, so effective tokens per call increased.
[01:02] Marco: side note on infra, our egress limits are still a question mark, security flagged possible peering caps if we go Dedicated into their VPC, I pinged them but no final answer yet.
[01:18] Dana: noted Marco, thanks. Sameer, take it away on the dashboard numbers.
[01:25] Sameer: okay share now, apologies if audio's rough. So slide 1 — overall pilot metrics week 3 vs week 2. Median latency at 1.8s for 512-token outputs on hosted variant, tokens/sec per dollar metric: with default batching we measured 3,200 tokens/sec per $1 for the hosted model baseline. After enabling the prefix KV caching we saw tokens/sec/$ move to ~3,900, that's the 22% improvement.
[02:05] Priya: can you explain how you're calculating tokens/sec/$? We want the exact formula cause our CFO is picky.
[02:12] Sameer: yeah, good call — it's (total tokens served in interval) / (elapsed seconds) divided by (dollars burned in interval). So tokens per second divided by dollars. We also normalize to $1 so it's tokens/sec per $1. There's a downloadable spreadsheet, Dana will share.
[02:28] Ellen: okay makes sense. On the client side we also tried increasing max_batch_size from 16 to 48 for a subset, throughput increased but tail latency for interactive UI users spiked. The UX team saw complaints at ~700ms tail beyond threshold.
[02:46] Dana: that matches other pilots, batching gives you unit econ wins but hurts interactivity. What about hybrid batching — separate low-latency route?
[02:55] Sameer: yeah we ran a route-split test: user-facing requests went to the low-latency pool (batch size 8, higher per-token cost) and background summarization to the high-throughput pool (batch 48). That split recovered interactivity and kept overall tokens/sec/$ up by ~15% vs baseline.
[03:18] Priya: interesting. Ellen, does your product have a clear separation of interactive vs background workloads?
[03:24] Ellen: sort of, most of our queries are real-time help desk stuff — that's interactive — but we also have nightly ingestion summaries which are perfect for background batching. We can route.
[03:33] Marco: about cost assumptions, are we including egress and storage overhead? Our bill shows some unexpected network egress when long contexts are sent repeatedly from the client.
[03:44] Sameer: good point, the tokens/sec/$ figure I'm quoting is compute-only — model serving cost. We can add a full unit-econ model that includes egress, storage (KV caches), and NLB/egress. Dana will attach an expanded sheet.
[03:58] Dana: we'll include a column for egress and one for expected storage ops on the KV cache.
[04:05] Priya: also security — the compliance team asked if logs can be partitioned per-customer and for audit log retention. Are those supported in Private?
[04:15] Dana: yes, on Redwood Private you get customer-separated audit logs, retention controls and KMS integration. For Hosted we provide redaction options but not full customer-managed KMS. Marco, is that a blocker?
[04:28] Marco: potential blocker if they insist on customer KMS, but we can probably start hosted and move to Private for high-volume tenants. We need to confirm SSO/SCIM too.
[04:39] Ellen: back to caching anomalies — we're seeing some cache key churn when emails include timestamps, like the prompts mutate slightly and caches miss. Any suggestions?
[04:48] Sameer: yes that's classic. Two quick tactics: prompt normalization (strip ephemeral tokens/timestamps) before hitting cache, and coarse-grained keys for multi-turn flows. We've seen up to 12% extra hits just by normalizing timestamps.
[05:02] Priya: can Redwood run a normalization pass as a proxy? It'd be easier than changing our client side.
[05:09] Dana: Redwood can do pre-processing at the gateway level — it's configurable but we recommend customers control normalization to avoid accidental PHI stripping. For this POC we can enable a light normalization rule set in the dev pilot environment.
[05:22] Ellen: good, please enable. We'll send examples of noisy prompts.
[05:28] Dana: noted. Sameer, any notes from the 32k long-context tests?
[05:33] Sameer: yeah, so the 32k workflow (logs ingestion + summarization) consumes a lot of KV cache memory. We tried 8-bit quant with sequence chunking. Cost improved but latency for the first token increased by ~30% because of chunk assembly overhead. The net tokens/sec/$ for the long-run batch job improved by ~40%, but interactive hits suffered.
[05:58] Marco: that sounds like the right trade for nightly jobs but not real time. We may need two model variants: quantized for nightly, full precision for real-time.
[06:08] Sameer: exactly. We also have an auto-fallback policy in Redwood: if the low-cost variant exceeds latency SLO then route to a higher-perf variant. That can be configured per-route.
[06:20] Priya: curious — how are you handling KV cache eviction and warmup? Our logs show a cold start penalty when a user initiates a long thread.
[06:31] Sameer: eviction is LRU by default with a small warmup window. For this pilot we can preload likely prefixes for known users — prefetch. We can also pin certain hot sessions to stay in memory during the session. There's a small cost for pinned memory but big latency gains.
[06:48] Ellen: prefetch sounds promising. We'll provide a list of ten heavy users to test pinning.
[06:53] Dana: nice. Let's talk about a concrete benchmark to run next week to close the loop on tokens/sec/$. Proposed: two runs — full-hosted baseline with KV enabled but no preprocessing, and hosted with gateway normalization + route split + pinning. Sameer to run both and give tokens/sec/$, p50/p95/p99 latencies, and cache hit-rates.
[07:17] Sameer: I propose also a 3rd run with quantized nightly variant to measure overall monthly cost impact; show delta if 20% of workload moves to nightly variant.
[07:27] Priya: that would help our finance team. Also, can you include a sensitivity analysis — if cache hit-rate drops to 40% what happens to cost?
[07:36] Sameer: yes we can run hit-rate sensitivity and produce a simple chart.
[07:40] Marco: networking again — if we move to Dedicated we need to know the minimum throughput SLAs and the burst behavior. Any documentation?
[07:49] Dana: yes, we'll share the Dedicated spec sheet — minimum reserved tokens/sec, autoscale burst config, and SLOs. I'll include it in the follow-up.
[07:58] Ellen: one more, in last week's run the tokens billed vs tokens observed had a small delta — billing showed ~2.3% more tokens. Is that quantization rounding or something else?
[08:10] Sameer: could be both rounding and double-encoding of certain unicode sequences; also, if the client sends both metadata and prompt as separate fields and we concat on-server it might cause double counting. We can audit by matching request IDs.
[08:25] Dana: action: Sameer + Marco to audit billing mismatch for the sample window and report findings.
[08:31] Marco: noted.
[08:33] Priya: any competitor notes we should consider? Our infra lead asked about Anthropic for safety features and OpenAI for general perf; curious if Redwood has any integration or comparisons.
[08:43] Dana: we did a perf/price matrix last quarter; I'll include a short competitor appendix. For safety features, Redwood supports response filters and can integrate with your existing safety pipeline.
[08:54] Ellen: okay, sounds good. Let's confirm next steps and owners.
[08:58] Dana: recap: Sameer runs three benchmark runs and sensitivity chart (due 2026-04-02). Dana sends cost model + Dedicated spec + competitor appendix (due 2026-04-01). Ellen provides noisy prompt samples and heavy-user list (due 2026-04-02). Marco confirms VPC/egress constraints and SCIM/SSO requirements (due 2026-04-05).
[09:22] Priya: that timeline works. Can we schedule the joint benchmark week now?
[09:27] Dana: sure, propose week of 2026-04-06, I'll send an invite with daily 30-min checkpoints.
[09:33] Marco: fine. One last quick item — can you share a template for post-run cost analysis? Our finance wants a standard sheet.
[09:40] Sameer: yes we have a template, I'll attach it with the benchmark results.
[09:44] Ellen: thanks everyone.
[09:46] Dana: thanks, we'll follow up with the artifacts. End of call.
